<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
This comment does useful work. It uses the microdata to establish things the working paper concealed or couldn't show:
- Seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals actually happened after the reduced schedule began.
- Manager ratings exceed record-based output in 19 of 23 organisations.
- Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.

Those findings are valuable and largely persuasive. But the conclusion goes far beyond what the analysis supports. The paper's own corrections leave a gain of about 11%. The novelty argument is speculative. And the comment reads the Varden trial selectively: the one randomised result that bears most directly on its central claim is omitted.

## Arithmetic check

- **Table 2:** 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 ✓. 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 ✓. 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 ✓.
- **Hours:** 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1% ✓. 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9% ✓.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, so about −2.6% ✓.

There are two errors:

**1. The hours decomposition doesn't add up.**
- Four days at about 8.7 hours (+0.7 on the scheduled 8) is 34.8 hours.
- Add 1.6 hours on the day off and you get about **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6.
- Measuring the +0.7 from the baseline actual day (8.06 hours) gives about 36.6.
- The reported 34.6 would need roughly +0.25 hours per day.

So either the daily increment or the day-off figure is wrong, or the components cover different subsets or weighting. Since the hours correction is the comment's largest single adjustment, this needs reconciling.

**2. The energy extrapolation is off.**
A straight line through +0.61 SD at month 3 and +0.29 SD at month 6 reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten." More importantly, two points can't establish a shape. The same line extended backwards gives +0.93 at month 0, when the baseline is 0 by definition, so the trajectory is plainly not linear. It could just as easily be levelling off.

## Major issues

**1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own results.**
- **What the results show:** After correcting output and hours, a 10.8% gain remains.
- **What the abstract says:** The problems "account for most" of the reported gain. That is roughly right: the corrections remove about half.
- **What the conclusion says:** The gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." The only bridge from 10.8% to zero is the novelty argument.
- **What Section 6 admits:** "Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one."

On the comment's own reasoning, then, novelty is unproven. That means "entirely an artifact" is also unproven. Placing the burden of proof on one side doesn't license asserting the opposite claim. The defensible conclusion is that "the corrected gain is roughly 11% in a non-random subset, of unknown durability."

**2. Attrition is listed as corrected, but it isn't.**
The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, which include attrition, gives 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is documented in Section 1 but never quantified. The comment needs:
- the employee counts of the nine withdrawers, since an employee-weighted mean may barely move if they were small;
- bounding analyses, such as worst-case imputation or Lee-type bounds, showing how much attrition could matter.

**3. Table 2 compares different samples row by row.**
The rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. Differences between rows therefore mix the effect of each correction with changes in sample composition. The data note concedes this, but the table still reads as a step-by-step decomposition. Compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations. That isolates each correction and shows whether the 17 started out unusual on the "as reported" measure.

**4. There is no uncertainty anywhere.**
The 10.8% rests on 17 organisations, and the retail figure of −11.2% on three, yet no estimate carries a CI. The comment criticises the original paper for weak inference while reporting point estimates only.

**5. The Varden trial is cited selectively.**
The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It never mentions the same trial's case-processing stratum. That stratum had:
- randomisation, so no self-selection;
- record-based output;
- timesheet hours;
- nine months of follow-up.

It found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. This addresses three of the comment's four explanations directly; only novelty remains, and over a longer window than Halden's. The comparison is striking:

| | Hours fall | Output | Gain per actual hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Halden, corrected (records + timesheets) | −13.9% | −4.6% | **+10.8%** |
| Varden case-processing (randomised) | −13% | −2.1% vs control | **+12.5%** |

Two very different designs converge on a gain of roughly 10–12% in office-type work. That is evidence *for* a real effect of modest size, the opposite of the comment's conclusion. Varden's counter result also has unresolved problems of its own: the abandonment figures are inconsistent with the size of the output fall, and there are only 5 v 5 clusters. "Most reliable finding in the literature" overstates it.

**6. The meetings critique misdescribes the Varden analysis.**
- **"Fitted to a subgroup":** The seven offices are the *entire* treated case-processing stratum, not a selected subset.
- **"Selected after the results were known":** Varden says the calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- **Caveats already made:** Varden stated that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test.

There is a real flaw the comment misses. Varden says meeting data were collected only in month six, yet it reports that offices that "cut" meetings most gained most. That requires pre-period data. The comment also ignores corroboration in the Halden interviews, where 47 of 58 managers mentioned reducing meetings. And it doesn't note why the hypothesis matters for its own argument: removing low-value time is a mechanism that would *not* fade with novelty.

**7. Novelty is argued from a proxy when direct data exist.**
The Halden output index was completed monthly, and record-based output presumably has a monthly series too. If gains are a novelty effect, output per hour should decline across months 1–6. The comment has the microdata and could test this directly instead of extrapolating self-reported energy. Energy is not output. Varden's nine-month window is also inconvenient for this argument: the energy extrapolation puts the return to baseline at around month 9, yet Varden still found a gain at month 9. The settings differ, but the comment should engage with this.

**8. The revenue section undercuts the comment's own case.**
- **Misframed in the abstract:** Revenue is listed among four problems that "account for most of the reported gain," but revenue is not part of the 23.4% calculation at all.
- **Its implication runs the other way:** A real revenue fall of 2.6% while actual hours fell about 14% implies real revenue per hour worked rose by roughly **13%**. That supports a per-hour gain rather than refuting it, though unchanged wage bills mean profitability is a separate question.
- **Deflator:** CPI is a crude deflator for organisational revenue; sector output prices would be better.

## Smaller points

- **"Overstates" assumes records are the truth.** The 3.8-point gap could also reflect records capturing only some output. And some record measures, such as "billable hours delivered," are partly inputs: for professional services they move mechanically with hours worked. Break the gap down by record type.
- **The baseline problem applies to the corrected figures too.** Halden's output baseline is the preceding six months, probably winter, not the same months a year earlier. That affects record-based output as much as manager ratings, and the comment doesn't address it.
- **Withdrawal reasons:** Six gave workload, two gave scheduling, and the ninth is unaccounted for.
- **Retail:** The sector-general critique is correct, and it matches my reading of the original. But three organisations is too few to give a sector figure much weight. The reversion pattern (5 of 11 customer-facing organisations reverted, against 0 of 50 others) is stronger evidence and goes unused.
- **Recommendations:** These are sound and worth keeping. Analysis of all enrolled organisations, including withdrawals, is a particularly important addition.

## Overall

The descriptive findings in Sections 1–4 belong in the literature, especially the evidence that withdrawals happened after the schedule began, contradicting the working paper. The inferential conclusion does not. A version that reports "a corrected gain of about 11% in office-type work, consistent with the Varden case-processing result, with durability unknown and coverage-bound work showing output losses" would be well supported and more useful than the current claim.

I can draft a referee report or a reply from the original authors' perspective, or put all three papers into one synthesis table.
